habitat: Red bats range across much of eastern North America, from southern Canada through the United States to Central America and Bermuda. They are highly migratory in northern areas, moving south for winter. They roost solitarily in the foliage of deciduous trees, particularly elms, oaks, maples, and fruit trees, hanging by one foot and camouflaged among leaves — appearing like dead leaves or pine cones. They are also found in orchards, urban parks, and forest edges. Unlike cave-dwelling bats, they rely entirely on tree foliage for shelter.
diet: Red bats are insectivorous, feeding on moths, beetles, flies, crickets, cicadas, plant-hoppers, and other flying insects. They are fast, agile fliers that hunt in open areas above tree canopies, along forest edges, and around streetlights where insects congregate. Using echolocation, they detect prey at distances of 5-10 meters. A single red bat may consume up to 500 insects in an hour, providing significant pest control services. They drink by skimming over the surface of ponds and streams.
behavior: Red bats are solitary except during mating and migration. Females form small maternity colonies of 3-5 but may roost alone with their young. A female typically gives birth to 2-4 pups — unusually large litters for a bat — which cling to her as she hangs upside down. They emerge to feed 1-2 hours after sunset, one of the earliest-emerging bat species. During migration, red bats may travel hundreds of kilometers and are frequently found resting on ships at sea or on buildings in urban areas, disoriented by lights.
facts: The red bat is one of the most beautifully colored bats in North America — males are a striking brick-red to rusty orange, while females are a duller chestnut with frosted tips. Their dense, soft fur extends to the upper surface of the tail membrane, an adaptation for cold weather. Unlike most bats, they do not hibernate in caves; they rely on their thick fur and leaf roosts to survive cold periods. They can live 12+ years in the wild and are important pollinators and seed dispersers in some parts of their range.
naming: Red bat names might reflect their brilliant color or nocturnal flight. Consider names like Rusty, Crimson, Ember, Maple, Autumn, Brick, Robin (for the red-breasted bird), Scarlet, Sienna, Foxy, Vesper (evening), or Flare.
